hub.h1: Practical guides for home practice and learning
hub.intro: Short, practical guides to help you choose a topic, build a home routine, understand progress, and combine digital practice, learning games, and worksheets when they fit.

sections.title: How to use these guides
paragraphs: Pick the guide that matches your goal right now. You can start with practice in one subject, build a home routine, understand a progress report, or choose a topic to strengthen. You do not need to do everything at once.

faq.q: How do I choose the right guide?
faq.a: Choose by your current goal: practice in a subject, building a home routine, understanding a report, or picking a topic to strengthen. Start with one guide and move to others later.

faq.q: Can I go from a guide straight to practice?
faq.a: Yes. Guides link to practice areas, learning games, parent reports, and worksheets based on the topic.

faq.q: Should I use several guides at once?
faq.a: You can, but it is better to start with one clear goal. After you see what works for your child, add another practice path or guide.

faq.q: Where can I see my child's progress?
faq.a: In the parent portal you can see completed activities, subjects and topics practiced, answers, and patterns over time.

footerCta.title: Choose a guide and take one step
footerCta.body: You do not need to change the whole learning routine in one day. Pick one goal, try it for a few days, and see what works for your child.

math-practice-at-home.h1: Math practice at home — how to start well
math-practice-at-home.intro: Home math practice works best when you choose a clear topic, match question level to grade, and stop before practice becomes overload. The goal is a steady rhythm that lets your child understand, try, and improve.

sections.title: Start with one topic
paragraphs: Choose a topic being taught now or one where your child needs more review. Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, fractions, decimals, percentages, and word problems use different kinds of thinking, so practice each topic separately before mixed practice.
bullets: Start with a few questions at the regular level.
Check whether difficulty comes from calculation, understanding the prompt, or order of operations.
Return to the same topic on another day before switching.

sections.title: How to respond to a mistake
paragraphs: Instead of giving the answer immediately, ask your child to explain what they tried. Go through the values together, mark the right operation, and solve one step at a time. When the same mistake repeats, choose more practice from the same family of questions.

sections.title: When to move to the next topic
paragraphs: Move on when your child answers most questions steadily and can explain their approach. Perfection is not required—understanding, consistency, and handling slightly different wording matter more.

sections.title: How to use Leo Kids
paragraphs: Choose your child's grade, open math, and pick one topic. After practice, check the report for correct answers, where reinforcement is needed, and what to practice next.

faq.q: How long should we practice?
faq.a: Length depends on age, topic, and focus. It is better to finish focused, good practice than to continue when your child is tired.

faq.q: Should we practice several topics together?
faq.a: Not at first. When one topic needs strengthening, start there and move to mixed practice only after a stable base.

faq.q: What if my child is guessing?
faq.a: Ask them to explain their approach, point to the values, and choose the operation before answering.

footerCta.title: Start with one math topic
footerCta.body: Choose grade, topic, and level, and let your child progress through questions matched to your practice choice.

no-print-worksheets.intro: You can practice at home directly from a computer, tablet, or phone. Digital practice and learning games let you start immediately, get new questions, and switch topics without preparing pages in advance. When paper helps, use Leo Kids worksheets.

sections.title: When is digital practice a good fit?
paragraphs: Digital practice fits when you want a quick start, immediate feedback, playful learning, or more independent practice for your child.
bullets: Quick entry by grade and subject.
Saved activity for tracking and reports.

sections.title: When is a worksheet a good fit?
paragraphs: A worksheet can help when your child prefers writing on paper, when you want screen-free time, when practicing structured writing and calculation, or when you want a sheet to reuse.

sections.title: You can combine both
paragraphs: You do not have to choose one path only. Start digitally, print a sheet for a topic that needs repetition, then return to a game or more online practice.

sections.title: How to start
paragraphs: Choose a subject and topic. For digital practice, go to the practice pages. For a worksheet, use the generator or pick from ready-made sheets.

faq.q: Do I have to print to use Leo Kids?
faq.a: No. You can use digital practice and games without printing.

faq.q: Are worksheets available too?
faq.a: Yes. Try the generator and choose from ready-made sheets with answer keys.

faq.q: Can we mix online practice and paper?
faq.a: Yes. Pick what fits the topic, your child, and the time you have.

footerCta.title: Choose the practice path that fits
footerCta.body: Start online or go to worksheets. Both options are available when you need them.

reading-practice-at-home.h1: Reading practice at home — accuracy, pace, and understanding
reading-practice-at-home.intro: Home reading practice does not have to be long. A short text at the right level can help your child read more accurately, recognize words faster, and understand the main idea.

sections.title: Choose a text that fits your child
paragraphs: A good text is one your child can read for most of it, but still includes a few words that need attention. A text that is too easy does not create practice; one that is too hard can turn reading into a struggle.

sections.title: What to focus on while reading
bullets: Returning to a word read incorrectly.
Understanding new words from the sentence.
Briefly explaining what happened in the text.

sections.title: How to correct without stopping every sentence
paragraphs: You do not have to fix every mistake immediately. When a mistake changes meaning, pause and return to the word. When your child self-corrects, let them continue. At the end, choose two or three words to read again.

sections.title: How to use practice on the site
paragraphs: On the reading page, choose a grade and start suitable practice. Questions help check word understanding, details from the text, and overall comprehension.

faq.q: Should we read the same text again?
faq.a: Yes. Rereading can improve accuracy and pace, as long as your child understands the text and is not only memorizing it.

faq.q: What about a hard word?
faq.a: Break it into parts, read it in the sentence, and explain its meaning briefly.

faq.q: Should we time reading?
faq.a: Not as a regular habit. Accuracy and understanding matter more than speed.

footerCta.title: Choose a short text and start reading
footerCta.body: Focused reading and comprehension practice can fit easily into a home routine.

reading-comprehension-at-home.h1: Reading comprehension at home — working with text and questions
reading-comprehension-at-home.intro: Comprehension is more than accurate reading. Your child needs to find details, understand connections, draw conclusions, and explain answers using the text.

sections.title: Start with the main idea
paragraphs: After reading, ask your child to say in one sentence what the text is about. If that is hard, return to the title, the first sentence, and the last sentence and find the central topic together.

sections.title: Question types worth practicing
bullets: Finding an explicit detail in the text.
Drawing a conclusion not stated directly.
Answering fully in the child's own words.

sections.title: Look for evidence in the text
paragraphs: When your child answers, ask them to show which sentence helped. That teaches them to support answers instead of relying on memory or guessing.

sections.title: What if the answer is partial?
paragraphs: Separate understanding the question from wording the answer. Highlight the question word, find the matching part of the text, then try a complete answer.

faq.q: Should we read the questions before the text?
faq.a: You can skim them briefly, but it is important to read the text fully—not only hunt for question words.

faq.q: How many questions should we do?
faq.a: A small number of different question types, with a full explanation of the approach, is better than many rushed answers.

faq.q: What is the difference between reading and comprehension?
faq.a: Reading focuses on recognizing words and reading accurately. Comprehension focuses on meaning, connections, and conclusions from the text.

footerCta.title: Read, find, and explain
footerCta.body: Choose a suitable text and practice one or two question types each time.

english-vocabulary-practice.intro: To remember a new English word, seeing it once is not enough. Read it, hear it, understand its meaning, and use it in several contexts.

sections.title: Practice a small group of words
paragraphs: Choose a small set of words from the same topic, such as family, home, food, colors, or school. A clear group helps your child connect words and remember them.

sections.title: Four ways to work with each word
bullets: Recognize the word in a sentence.
Return to the word on another day.

sections.title: Do not practice translation only
paragraphs: Translation is an important step, but the goal is for your child to recognize the word in a sentence. Ask what fits the word, what its opposite is, or when it is used.

sections.title: How to use Leo Kids
paragraphs: Choose a grade, open English, and pick vocabulary or a suitable topic. You can return for more practice and meet words in a different order.

faq.q: How many new words should we practice?
faq.a: Start with a small group you can review several times during the week.

faq.q: Do we have to write every word?
faq.a: Writing can help, but reading, saying, and using the word in a sentence matter too.

faq.q: What if a word is forgotten again?
faq.a: Bring it back into the practice group and use it in another context.

footerCta.title: Choose a word group and start practicing
footerCta.body: Reading, meaning, and use in sentences help turn a new word into a familiar one.

learning-games-at-home.h1: How to combine learning games at home
learning-games-at-home.intro: Learning games can turn review into something your child wants to finish. For a game to support learning, choose one that fits the subject, topic, and level.

sections.title: Choose a game by goal
paragraphs: Before starting, decide what you want to practice. You can pick a game for calculation, reading, vocabulary, science, or thinking. When the goal is clear, it is easier to see whether the game really helps.

sections.title: What to do during the game
bullets: Let your child try on their own.
Pause only when the same difficulty repeats.
Ask them to explain a choice or answer.
Notice whether they act from understanding or guessing.
Stop when the goal is reached.

sections.title: Combine games with more practice
paragraphs: After the game, move to a few questions on the same topic, or return to the game another day. The mix helps your child meet the same idea in a different form.

sections.title: How to use games on the site
paragraphs: Choose a game that fits the subject and level. Games combine educational tasks, challenges, coins, and progress inside the activity.

faq.q: Can a game replace all practice?
faq.a: A game is one way to practice. For some topics, combine questions, reading, writing, or a worksheet too.

faq.q: How do I know a game fits?
faq.a: Your child should understand the task and handle a reasonable challenge without guessing most answers.

faq.q: What if my child focuses only on rewards?
faq.a: Pause sometimes and ask what they learned or how they solved a task.

footerCta.title: Choose a game that fits your goal
footerCta.body: A good game combines fun with clear practice of a topic your child can understand and progress in.

math-games-for-kids.h1: Math games for kids — practice through challenge
math-games-for-kids.intro: Math games let children practice operations, numbers, and thinking inside a clear task. Choose a game that fits a topic your child knows and a skill you want to strengthen.

sections.title: Keep the math goal clear
paragraphs: Even when a game has characters, coins, or levels, ask your child how they reached an answer. Explaining helps distinguish understanding from guessing.

sections.title: Match the challenge level
paragraphs: A game that is too easy does not create new learning; one that is too hard can cause frustration. Choose a level where your child succeeds on most tasks but still has to think.

sections.title: After the game
paragraphs: Choose a few questions on the same topic and check whether your child uses the same approach outside the game. That turns the game into part of broader practice.

faq.q: Which game fits my child?
faq.a: Choose by grade, the topic your child is learning, and a difficulty level where they can work independently.

faq.q: Should we play the same game again?
faq.a: Yes, especially when the game shows changing tasks and helps improve accuracy and pace.

faq.q: What if my child is guessing?
faq.a: Ask them to pause and explain the operation or relationship between the numbers.

footerCta.title: Practice math through games
footerCta.body: Choose a familiar topic, match the level, and ask your child to explain their approach alongside the game.

parent-progress-tracking.h1: How to read your child's progress reports
parent-progress-tracking.intro: A progress report helps you see what your child practiced, where they succeed, and where difficulty repeats. The goal is not one score—it is a broader picture over time.

sections.title: What to check in a report
bullets: Which subjects and topics were practiced.
How much time was spent learning.

sections.title: Do not rely on one session
paragraphs: One practice result can be affected by tiredness, lack of focus, or first exposure to a topic. Check whether the same pattern repeats across several activities.

sections.title: Separate temporary difficulty from a steady pattern
paragraphs: One mistake does not require an immediate plan change. When the same mistake repeats on the same question type, choose focused practice and check again after a few days.

sections.title: What to do after reading a report
paragraphs: Choose one action: review a topic, move to a better-matched level, add practice, or have a short conversation about how your child solved questions.

faq.q: Does a low score mean my child does not know the topic?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Look at mistake types and results across several practice sessions.

faq.q: How often should I check reports?
faq.a: After several activities or about once a week, depending on how often you use the site.

faq.q: What matters more—time or accuracy?
faq.a: Both provide information, but understanding the approach and mistake types matters more than one number alone.

footerCta.title: Use the report to understand what happened in practice
footerCta.body: Review topics, spot patterns, and choose one next action.

home-practice-routine.h1: How to build a home practice routine that fits
home-practice-routine.intro: A good home routine does not have to look the same every day. It should be clear, doable, and include tasks that fit your time, focus, and the topic your child needs.

sections.title: Set a steady starting point
paragraphs: Choose a time when your child is relatively free and not too tired. Fixed days can help, but leave flexibility on busy days or when your child needs a break.

sections.title: Choose one goal per session
bullets: A quick check of a topic practiced earlier.

sections.title: End clearly
paragraphs: Your child should know in advance what needs to be finished. When the task is done, stop. A clear ending builds success and willingness to return.

sections.title: Adjust the routine as progress changes
paragraphs: If a topic feels stable, move to the next one. If difficulty repeats, change the practice type or choose a better-matched level.

faq.q: Do we have to practice every day?
faq.a: No. A steady routine that fits your family matters more than a plan you cannot keep.

faq.q: What about a busy day?
faq.a: Choose a shorter task or postpone practice without turning the routine into punishment.

faq.q: Should my child choose?
faq.a: You can let them choose between two tasks that fit the goal you set.

footerCta.title: Build a routine you can keep
footerCta.body: Choose a suitable time, one goal, and a clear ending for each session.

how-to-follow-child-progress.h1: How to choose the next topic to strengthen
how-to-follow-child-progress.intro: Choosing a topic to strengthen starts with spotting a pattern. Look for difficulty that repeats across several questions or sessions—not a single mistake. Then choose focused practice and check again.

sections.title: Three sources of information
bullets: Your child's explanation of how they tried to solve.

sections.title: Define the topic precisely
paragraphs: Instead of a broad area like math or reading, name a focused topic: vertical addition, long multiplication, following instructions, finding details in a text, or vocabulary in a specific theme.

sections.title: Choose suitable practice
paragraphs: Start at a level where your child can succeed on most questions. If it is too hard, return to a more basic step. If it is too easy, move to a harder level or question type.

sections.title: Check whether something changed
paragraphs: After several practice sessions, return to the same question type and check whether your child answers more steadily and can explain their approach.

faq.q: Should I always pick the topic with the lowest score?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Also look at how many questions were answered, what kind of difficulty appeared, and whether it repeated in later practice.

faq.q: How many topics should we strengthen at once?
faq.a: Start with one topic or two closely related ones so practice stays clear.

faq.q: When do we move to another topic?
faq.a: When your child shows steadier understanding and can handle questions worded differently.

footerCta.title: Spot a pattern and choose a focused topic
footerCta.body: Use reports, answers, and your child's explanation to choose the next step.

faq.q: Which grades is practice designed for?
faq.a: Practice is designed for grades 1–6, with each subject showing topics suited to the grade you select.

faq.q: Do I have to print?
faq.a: No. You can practice online, play learning games, or use a worksheet when that fits your routine.

faq.q: How do I choose a topic?
faq.a: Pick what is being taught now, a topic your child wants to review, or use parent reports to decide what to practice next.

footerCta.title: Choose a subject and start practicing

math.h1: Math practice by grade and topic
math.intro: In Leo Kids, children can practice math by grade, topic, and difficulty. Questions vary between sessions and support calculation, understanding, and problem solving.

sections.title: How do I start?
paragraphs: Choose a grade, open the math topic you want, and start at the regular level. After a few questions, check whether the level fits and continue with more practice.

sections.title: How do I choose a topic?
paragraphs: Pick a topic being taught now, one where mistakes appeared, or a skill your child wants to strengthen. When a topic feels stable, move to mixed practice.

gradeSections.title: Grades 1–2
gradeSections.text: Numbers, counting, basic addition and subtraction, comparing quantities, and short exercises.

gradeSections.title: Grades 3–4
gradeSections.text: Strengthening operations, multiplication and division, word problems, and practice that builds understanding—not just speed.

gradeSections.title: Grades 5–6
gradeSections.text: Fractions, percentages, decimals, more complex problems, and topics that require step-by-step thinking.

faq.q: Do questions change between sessions?
faq.a: Yes. Activities are drawn from a question bank and can vary between practice runs.

faq.q: Are there different levels?
faq.a: Yes. Topics offer regular and advanced levels based on content and grade.

faq.q: Can I print exercises?
faq.a: Yes. On the worksheets page you can create a sheet or choose a ready-made one with answers.

footerCta.title: Choose a math topic
footerCta.body: Start with focused practice and continue based on your child's progress.

reading.h1: Reading comprehension practice for elementary learners
reading.intro: On the reading page, children practice word recognition, accurate reading, sentence understanding, finding details, and drawing conclusions from grade-appropriate texts.

sections.title: How do I start?
paragraphs: Choose a grade and start with a text where your child can read most of the words. After reading, move to the questions and ask your child to explain how they found each answer.

sections.title: What if there is difficulty?
paragraphs: If the challenge is reading the words, return to short, focused reading. If the challenge is understanding the question, highlight the question word and find the matching part of the text.

gradeSections.title: Grades 1–2
gradeSections.text: Early reading, short words and sentences, basic understanding, and simple questions.

gradeSections.title: Grades 3–4
gradeSections.text: Short texts, comprehension questions, finding information, and brief written answers.

gradeSections.title: Grades 5–6
gradeSections.text: Longer texts, drawing conclusions, more detailed answers, and stronger comprehension accuracy.

faq.q: Is this Hebrew language reading?
faq.a: No. This page focuses on English reading comprehension—short texts and questions that build understanding and fluency.

faq.q: Are texts matched to grade?
faq.a: Yes. Practice is selected by grade and activity difficulty.

faq.q: How do I know if my child understood?
faq.a: Ask them to explain the main idea and point to the part of the text that helped them answer.

footerCta.title: Choose a text and start reading
footerCta.body: Practice accurate reading, comprehension, and explaining answers from the text.

english.h1: English practice by grade and topic
english.intro: English practice includes phonics, vocabulary, sentences, grammar, reading, and following instructions. Choose a grade and topic and work on one skill per activity.

sections.title: How do I choose a topic?
paragraphs: In younger grades, start with letters, sounds, and basic words. Later, focus on vocabulary, sentences, grammar, and reading.

sections.title: How do I reinforce a new word?
paragraphs: Read the word, understand its meaning, recognize it in a sentence, and use it in another context.

gradeSections.title: Grades 1–2
gradeSections.text: First exposure to words, sounds, letters, and short sentences.

gradeSections.title: Grades 3–4
gradeSections.text: Expanding vocabulary, understanding sentences, short reading, and basic structure practice.

gradeSections.title: Grades 5–6
gradeSections.text: Short texts, simple writing, more advanced grammar, and context-based understanding.

faq.q: Is there phonics practice?
faq.a: Yes. Phonics activities are available for younger grades.

faq.q: Can we practice vocabulary?
faq.a: Yes. Choose activities for words, meaning, and use in sentences.

faq.q: Are there English worksheets?
faq.a: Yes. The worksheets page includes ready-made sheets and a generator to try.

footerCta.title: Choose an English topic
footerCta.body: Start with words and sounds, then move to sentences, grammar, and reading.

geometry.h1: Geometry practice by grade and topic
geometry.intro: Geometry practice covers shapes, lines, angles, perimeter, area, solids, symmetry, circles, volume, and Pythagoras. Questions combine identification, calculation, and diagrams by topic.

sections.title: How do I start?
paragraphs: Choose a grade and topic. For identification questions, look at labels on the diagram. For calculation questions, write the given values and choose the right operation or formula.

sections.title: How do I use the diagram?
paragraphs: The diagram shows the shape, measurements, and labels needed to solve the problem. Read the question too—do not rely only on how the shape looks.

gradeSections.title: Grades 1–2
gradeSections.text: Identifying shapes, telling shapes apart, lines, and basic properties.

gradeSections.title: Grades 3–4
gradeSections.text: Measurement, perimeter, angles, and properties of familiar shapes.

gradeSections.title: Grades 5–6
gradeSections.text: Area, relationships between shapes, more advanced topics, and step-by-step reasoning.

faq.q: Do questions include diagrams?
faq.a: Yes. Suitable questions include shape and solid diagrams with measurements and labels.

faq.q: Can we practice area and perimeter?
faq.a: Yes. Topics include area, perimeter, measurements, and grade-appropriate calculations.

faq.q: Are there geometry worksheets?
faq.a: Yes. Ready-made sheets and a generator are available on the worksheets page.

footerCta.title: Choose a geometry topic
footerCta.body: Practice identification, drawing, and calculation with topic-matched questions.

science.intro: Science practice in Leo Kids helps children review concepts, understand processes, and apply knowledge in questions. Activities combine facts, comparison, cause and effect, and understanding phenomena.

sections.title: How do we practice science?
paragraphs: Choose a topic, read each question, and look for the concept or process it is based on. When there are several options, eliminate answers that do not fit the facts in the question.

sections.title: More than memorizing facts
paragraphs: Ask your child to explain why an answer is correct, what causes a process, and how the result changes when a condition changes.

gradeSections.title: Grades 1–2
gradeSections.text: Introduction to animals, plants, the human body, and the nearby environment.

gradeSections.title: Grades 3–4
gradeSections.text: Deeper understanding of materials, natural processes, living systems, and environmental phenomena.

gradeSections.title: Grades 5–6
gradeSections.text: More advanced topics such as earth and space, environment, experiments, and structured scientific thinking.

faq.q: Does practice include comprehension questions?
faq.a: Yes. Alongside facts and concepts, there are questions that ask children to explain relationships and processes.

faq.q: How do I choose a topic?
faq.a: Pick what is being taught now or a topic your child wants to review.

faq.q: Do activities change?
faq.a: Yes. Different practice runs can show different questions from the topic bank.

footerCta.title: Choose a science topic
footerCta.body: Review concepts and use them to explain processes and phenomena.

games.h1: Learning games for kids by subject and level
games.intro: Leo Kids learning games combine tasks in math, English, science, and reading comprehension inside playful activities. Each game has a clear goal, questions, and challenges matched to the chosen level.

sections.title: What can children practice in games?
How do I choose a game?
paragraphs: Pick by the subject and topic your child wants to practice. Start at a level where they understand the task and can progress without guessing most answers.

sections.title: What after the game?
paragraphs: Ask what the main challenge was, which question was hard, and what strategy helped them succeed.

gradeSections.title: Grades 1–2
gradeSections.text: Games with short instructions and tasks for identification, matching, calculation, reading, and vocabulary at a young-learner level.

gradeSections.title: Grades 3–4
gradeSections.text: Games that combine multiplication, division, text understanding, vocabulary, science, task solving, and multi-step progress.

gradeSections.title: Grades 5–6
gradeSections.text: Games with harder challenges, problem solving, accuracy, decision making, and subject-based knowledge.

faq.q: Do games include educational questions?
faq.a: Yes. Games combine questions and tasks as part of the activity.

faq.q: Are there different levels?
faq.a: Yes. Games adjust task types and challenge level for different age groups and levels.

faq.q: Can children play as guests?
faq.a: Access options depend on system settings and the game selected.

footerCta.title: Choose a game and start a learning challenge
footerCta.body: Match the game to subject and level and let your child progress through tasks and questions.

no-print.h1: Digital practice for kids — no printing required
no-print.intro: Start practice directly on the site, choose a subject and topic, and get questions and activities without preparing pages in advance. Digital games and practice are available by grade and subject.

sections.title: What can you do online?
bullets: Practice questions by subject and topic.
Save activity for reports and tracking.

sections.title: Start without prep
paragraphs: Choose a subject, grade, and topic and begin. No need to download a file or prepare materials first.

sections.title: Print when it helps
paragraphs: When you want to work on paper, go to the worksheets page, use the generator, or choose from ready-made sheets.

gradeSections.title: Grades 1–2
gradeSections.text: Short activities in math, reading, language, and learning games open directly on the site with clear instructions for young learners.

gradeSections.title: Grades 3–4
gradeSections.text: Choose a subject and topic, practice changing questions, mix in learning games, and return for more activity as needed.

gradeSections.title: Grades 5–6
gradeSections.text: Digital practice supports focused topics, harder questions, problem solving, reading, language, and additional subjects.

faq.q: Do I need a printer?
faq.a: No. Digital practice and games work directly on the site.

faq.q: Is there also a printable option?
faq.a: Yes. On the worksheets page you can create a sheet, preview it, and print when helpful.

faq.q: Is activity saved?
faq.a: In the parent portal you can track activities, subjects, and topics practiced.

footerCta.title: Start practicing on the site
footerCta.body: Choose a subject and topic, or go to worksheets when paper practice fits better.

parent-reports.h1: Parent progress reports — see what your child practiced
parent-reports.intro: Parent reports summarize activities your child completed, subjects and topics practiced, answers, and progress over time.

sections.title: What can you see in reports?
Standard and detailed reports
paragraphs: The standard report gives a quick picture of activity. The detailed report lets you go deeper into topics, questions, and patterns that repeat across practice.

sections.title: How to use the information
paragraphs: After reading a report, choose one next step: review a topic, add practice, change level, or move to the next topic.

gradeSections.title: General
gradeSections.text: Reports are based on your child's actual activity on the site.

gradeSections.title: By subject
gradeSections.text: Reports can reflect practiced areas such as math, English, geometry, and science—based on activity and available content.

faq.q: Does a report show only a score?
faq.a: No. Reports include topics, activity, answers, and patterns over time.

faq.q: When should I check a report?
faq.a: After several activities or when you want to choose a new topic to practice.

faq.q: Can I see topics to strengthen?
faq.a: Reports can help identify topics where difficulty repeats and choose suitable practice.

footerCta.title: Turn activity into useful information
footerCta.body: See what your child practiced, spot patterns, and choose the next step.

practiceHubCards.title: Learning games

practiceHubCards.title: Parent reports

practiceHubCards.title: Worksheets
practiceHubCards.blurb: Worksheet generator, ready-made sheets, answer keys, and print when helpful.

worksheets.h1: Printable worksheets for kids — practice, print when helpful, or combine with online learning
worksheets.intro: On this page you can create a demo sheet with 8 exercises or choose from 30 ready worksheets in math, geometry, and English. Preview each sheet, print it, and open an answer key.

sections.title: How do I create a demo sheet?
paragraphs: Pick a subject and grade, then create a short demo with 8 exercises. One topic per subject and grade is open for the demo; other topics show what is available in the full parent portal.

sections.title: Ready worksheets by grade
paragraphs: Choose from 30 ready sheets, filter by subject, grade, and level, open the sheet, and print when it fits your routine. Each sheet can have a separate answer key.

sections.title: Practice without printing too
paragraphs: Worksheets are an extra option alongside digital practice and games. Pick what fits the topic, your child, and the time you have.

sections.title: What does the full parent portal include?
paragraphs: In the full parent portal you can create unlimited worksheets, choose every available topic, and generate fresh sheets again and again. Sheets are rebuilt from the question bank and change between runs.

sections.title: Answer keys for home checking
paragraphs: You can open a separate answer key after creating a sheet. The demo includes answers for all 8 exercises; ready sheets include answers according to each sheet's structure.

faq.q: Do I need to sign up to try this?
faq.a: No. The demo generator and ready sheets are available without logging in.

faq.q: How many exercises are in the demo sheet?
faq.a: The demo sheet has 8 exercises. Ready sheets keep their full structure.

faq.q: Are answer keys available?
faq.a: Yes. You can open a separate answer key for the demo and for each ready sheet.

faq.q: Do we have to print?
faq.a: No. You can practice online in Leo Kids and use a worksheet when printing helps.

faq.q: Do the sheets change?
faq.a: Sheets created in the generator are rebuilt from the question bank and can differ between runs.

footerCta.title: Want to create more sheets and unlock every topic?
footerCta.body: In the full parent portal you can create unlimited worksheets, pick additional topics, and combine sheets with digital practice and progress insights.
